promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

learningObjectives.title: The relationship between language and thought (Piaget and the Sapir-Whorf hypothesis)
Differences between human and animal communication

questions.q: According to Piaget, what is the relationship between language and thought?
options: Thought develops first and language reflects it
Language and thought are completely unrelated
Language must fully develop before thought can begin
questions.explain: Piaget argued that cognitive development (thought) comes first and language simply labels the concepts a child has already understood.

questions.q: What does the Sapir-Whorf hypothesis claim about language?
options: Language has no effect on how we think
Thought develops before and independently of language
Language influences or determines the way we think
All languages produce identical patterns of thought
questions.explain: Sapir and Whorf proposed that the language a person speaks shapes how they perceive and think about the world.

questions.q: Which statement best describes the strong version of the Sapir-Whorf hypothesis (linguistic determinism)?
options: Language only slightly nudges our thinking
Language completely determines and limits thought
questions.explain: The strong version, linguistic determinism, claims that thought is entirely controlled by the language available to a person.

questions.q: The idea that language influences but does not completely control thought is known as:
questions.explain: Linguistic relativity is the weaker version, stating that language affects (but does not fully dictate) how we think.

questions.q: A community whose language has many separate words for different types of snow tends to notice more distinctions between them than English speakers. This best supports:
questions.explain: Differences in vocabulary affecting perception and recognition illustrate the Sapir-Whorf idea that language shapes thought.

questions.q: A toddler understands the concept of a 'dog' before she can say the word. This observation fits best with:
options: Piaget's theory that thought precedes language
questions.explain: For Piaget, the child forms the concept (schema) first, then acquires the word to describe it.

questions.q: Von Frisch's classic study of animal communication investigated which species?
questions.explain: Von Frisch studied how honeybees communicate the location of food through movement patterns.

questions.q: In Von Frisch's research, what does the bee's 'waggle dance' communicate to other bees?
options: Only the type of flower found
The distance and direction of a food source
A warning of an approaching predator
The identity of the queen bee
questions.explain: The angle and duration of the waggle run indicate the direction (relative to the sun) and distance of food.

questions.q: Which feature of human communication is generally absent from animal communication?
questions.explain: Human language shows plasticity, allowing new, flexible and creative combinations, unlike the largely fixed signals of animals.

questions.q: A bee performs a 'round dance' on returning to the hive. This most likely indicates that food is:
questions.explain: The round dance signals that a food source is nearby, whereas the waggle dance is used for more distant food.

questions.q: A male peacock spreads its large, colourful tail feathers. Which function of animal communication does this best illustrate?
questions.explain: The display is used to attract a mate, serving the reproductive function of animal communication.

questions.q: A vervet monkey gives a specific loud call when it spots an eagle, causing others to take cover. This communication mainly serves which function?
questions.explain: Alarm calls that warn others of danger help the group avoid predators, serving the survival function.

questions.q: Non-verbal communication is best defined as:
options: Communicating without the use of words
questions.explain: Non-verbal communication conveys messages without words, e.g. through eye contact, posture and gestures.

questions.q: Which of the following is a recognised function of eye contact?
questions.explain: Eye contact helps regulate conversational turn-taking, as well as signalling attraction and expressing emotion.

questions.q: During a chat, one person unconsciously copies the other's relaxed, leaning posture. This is an example of:
questions.explain: Postural echo is the mirroring of another person's posture and usually signals friendliness and rapport.

questions.q: Sitting with tightly folded arms and crossed legs is an example of closed posture, which typically signals:
questions.explain: Closed posture tends to communicate defensiveness, rejection or disagreement, unlike open, welcoming posture.

questions.q: Which of these is a factor that influences how much personal space people prefer?
questions.explain: Personal space is affected by factors such as culture, status and gender/sex differences.

questions.q: Whose evolutionary theory explains non-verbal behaviour as innate and adaptive?
questions.explain: Darwin's evolutionary theory argues that many non-verbal behaviours are innate, inherited and served a survival advantage.

questions.q: Which finding provides the strongest evidence that some non-verbal behaviour is innate?
options: Facial expressions of emotion are recognised across all cultures
People learn new slang throughout life
questions.explain: Universal facial expressions, plus evidence from newborns and sensory-deprived (e.g. blind) people, suggest an innate basis.

questions.q: A study finds that hand gestures used to greet others differ greatly from one country to another. This best supports the view that some non-verbal communication is:
options: Learned through the environment and culture
questions.explain: Cross-cultural differences in gestures indicate that some non-verbal behaviour is learned rather than innate.
